A day on Venus is longer than its year. It takes 243 Earth days to spin once, but only 225 to orbit the Sun.
A teaspoon of neutron star would weigh about a billion tonnes on Earth.
Venus spins backwards compared with most planets. On Venus, the Sun rises in the west.
Jupiter is so big that all the other planets in the solar system could fit inside it.
Saturn is less dense than water. In a big enough bathtub, it would float.
The footprints left on the Moon by Apollo astronauts could last millions of years. There's no wind to blow them away.
A year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the tallest volcano in the solar system, about two and a half times taller than Mount Everest.
The Sun makes up about 99.8% of all the mass in our solar system.
Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth.
There are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on all of Earth's beaches, by most estimates.
Neptune was the first planet found by maths. Astronomers predicted where it should be before anyone saw it.
Uranus is tipped over on its side. It basically rolls around the Sun.
One million Earths could fit inside the Sun.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than Earth that has been raging for centuries.
Space is completely silent. With no air to carry sound waves, there's nothing to hear.
Mars has two tiny moons, Phobos and Deimos. Their names mean "fear" and "dread."
Mars looks red because its surface is covered in iron oxide. Basically, the planet is rusty.
The International Space Station orbits Earth about every 90 minutes. Astronauts see around 16 sunrises a day.
The Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth, by about 3.8 centimetres a year.
We always see the same side of the Moon. It spins exactly once for every trip around Earth.
Our galaxy, the Milky Way, is about 100,000 light-years across.
The Andromeda Galaxy is on a collision course with the Milky Way. They're expected to merge in about 4 to 5 billion years.
Saturn's rings are mostly made of ice, with some rock and dust.
Saturn's rings are enormous but thin. In many places they're only about 10 metres thick.
A black hole's gravity is so strong that not even light can escape once it crosses the event horizon.
At the centre of our galaxy sits a supermassive black hole called Sagittarius A*. It's about 4 million times the mass of the Sun.
In 2019, scientists released the first-ever image of a black hole, in the galaxy M87.
The Voyager 1 probe, launched in 1977, is the most distant human-made object, more than 20 billion kilometres away.
Voyager 1 and 2 each carry a golden record with sounds and images from Earth, in case aliens ever find them.
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
Pluto has a giant heart-shaped plain on its surface, nicknamed Tombaugh Regio.
A day on Jupiter lasts only about 10 hours. It's the fastest-spinning planet.
Venus is the hottest planet in the solar system, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun. Its thick atmosphere traps heat.
The surface of Venus is hot enough to melt lead.
Jupiter has dozens of moons. Ganymede, the largest, is bigger than the planet Mercury.
Saturn's moon Titan has lakes and rivers, but they're filled with liquid methane, not water.
Jupiter's moon Europa likely has a huge ocean of liquid water under its icy crust.
Saturn's moon Enceladus shoots jets of water vapour and ice into space from its south pole.
The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old, roughly halfway through its life.
In about 5 billion years, the Sun will swell into a red giant.
Neutron stars can spin hundreds of times per second.
The coldest known place in the universe is the Boomerang Nebula, at about −272 °C, just one degree above absolute zero.
Astronauts can grow up to about 5 centimetres taller in space because their spines stretch without gravity.
In microgravity, flames burn in a round ball instead of a teardrop shape.
The Moon has quakes too. Scientists call them moonquakes.
Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so its temperature swings from about 430 °C in the day to about −180 °C at night.
Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system, reaching over 2,000 km/h.
The Kármán line, about 100 km up, is commonly used as the boundary where space begins.
Light from the nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, takes about 4.2 years to reach us.
When you look at the stars, you're seeing them as they were when the light left them, sometimes thousands of years ago.
A light-year is a distance, not a time. It's how far light travels in a year: about 9.46 trillion kilometres.
Halley's Comet passes Earth about every 76 years. It's next due in 2061.
Shooting stars aren't stars. They're tiny bits of space dust burning up in our atmosphere.
Most meteors are no bigger than a grain of sand.
The Sun's core reaches about 15 million °C.
Sunlight reaching you today was made in the Sun's core long ago. Energy can take over 100,000 years to work its way out to the surface.
Jupiter has faint rings too. They're just much harder to see than Saturn's.
Every planet in our solar system except Mercury and Venus has at least one moon.
A full spacesuit for a NASA spacewalk is a mini spacecraft with its own oxygen, cooling and power.
The first animal to orbit Earth was a dog named Laika, in 1957.
Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space on 12 April 1961.
Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon on 20 July 1969.
Twelve people have walked on the Moon, all between 1969 and 1972.
Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space in 1963.
Rakesh Sharma became the first Indian in space in 1984. Asked how India looked from space, he said: "Saare Jahan Se Achha."
India's Chandrayaan-3 made the first soft landing near the Moon's south pole in August 2023.
India's Mangalyaan reached Mars orbit on its first attempt in 2014.
The Hubble Space Telescope has been orbiting Earth since 1990.
The James Webb Space Telescope sits about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth.
Mars has the biggest canyon in the solar system, Valles Marineris. It would stretch across most of the USA.
Mars has seasons, like Earth, because its axis is tilted by a similar amount.
Olympus Mons is so wide that if you stood on its edge, the summit would be beyond the horizon.
Comets have tails that always point away from the Sun, pushed by the solar wind.
The asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter is mostly empty space. Spacecraft fly through it without hitting anything.
There may be more planets than stars in the Milky Way.
Astronomers have confirmed more than 5,000 planets orbiting other stars.
The universe is about 13.8 billion years old.
The observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across.
Most of the universe is made of dark energy and dark matter, which we can't see directly.
Ordinary matter, everything we can see and touch, makes up only about 5% of the universe.
Mercury is the smallest planet in the solar system, only slightly larger than our Moon.
Mercury has ice inside permanently shadowed craters near its poles, despite being closest to the Sun.
Venus is the brightest planet in our night sky, often called the morning or evening star.
Venus's clouds are made largely of sulfuric acid.
The air pressure on Venus's surface is about 90 times that on Earth, like being 900 metres underwater.
Soviet Venera landers sent back the first pictures from Venus's surface in the 1970s, before being crushed and cooked.
Earth is the only planet known to have plate tectonics today.
Mars is about half the size of Earth.
Gravity on Mars is about 38% of Earth's. You could jump nearly three times higher there.
A day on Mars, called a sol, is about 24 hours and 39 minutes long.
A year on Mars lasts about 687 Earth days.
Mars has the biggest dust storms in the solar system. Some cover the entire planet.
Mars has polar ice caps made of water ice and frozen carbon dioxide.
NASA's Perseverance rover landed on Mars in 2021, carrying a small helicopter called Ingenuity.
Ingenuity made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet in April 2021.
The Curiosity rover has been exploring Mars since 2012.
Mars once had rivers and lakes. Rovers have found ancient riverbeds and deltas.
Phobos, Mars's larger moon, is slowly spiralling inwards and may break apart or crash in tens of millions of years.
Jupiter is more than 300 times the mass of Earth.
Jupiter has the strongest magnetic field of any planet.
Jupiter's moon Io is the most volcanically active place in the solar system.
Io's volcanoes are powered by tidal squeezing from Jupiter's gravity.
Jupiter's moon Callisto is one of the most heavily cratered objects in the solar system.
Ganymede is the only moon known to have its own magnetic field.
Jupiter acts like a cosmic vacuum cleaner, pulling in or flinging away many comets and asteroids.
In 1994, pieces of comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 crashed into Jupiter, leaving dark scars bigger than Earth.
Saturn has more known moons than any other planet, well over a hundred.
Saturn's hexagon is a six-sided jet stream pattern at its north pole, wider than Earth.
Saturn is so far away that sunlight there is about 1% as bright as on Earth.
NASA's Cassini spacecraft studied Saturn for 13 years before diving into the planet in 2017.
The Huygens probe landed on Titan in 2005, the most distant landing ever made.
Titan is the only moon with a thick atmosphere.
Titan's atmosphere is so thick and its gravity so low that a human could fly there with wings strapped to their arms.
Saturn's moon Iapetus has one bright side and one dark side, like a yin-yang.
Saturn's moon Mimas has a giant crater that makes it look like the Death Star.
Uranus was the first planet discovered with a telescope, by William Herschel in 1781.
Uranus is the coldest planetary atmosphere in the solar system, dropping to about −224 °C.
Uranus has faint rings, discovered in 1977.
Uranus's moons are named after characters from Shakespeare and Alexander Pope.
Neptune takes about 165 Earth years to orbit the Sun once.
Since its discovery in 1846, Neptune completed its first full orbit only in 2011.
Neptune's largest moon, Triton, orbits backwards compared with the planet's spin.
Triton has geysers that shoot nitrogen gas into its thin atmosphere.
Triton is slowly spiralling towards Neptune and may one day be torn apart into rings.
Only one spacecraft, Voyager 2, has ever visited Uranus and Neptune.
Pluto is smaller than Earth's Moon.
Pluto's largest moon, Charon, is so big that the two orbit a point in space between them.
NASA's New Horizons flew past Pluto in 2015, giving us the first close-up pictures.
Pluto has mountains of water ice as tall as the Rockies.
A year on Pluto lasts about 248 Earth years.
Since its discovery in 1930, Pluto hasn't yet completed a full orbit of the Sun.
Ceres, in the asteroid belt, is a dwarf planet too.
Eris, a dwarf planet beyond Pluto, is about the same size as Pluto but more massive.
The Moon is about a quarter of Earth's width.
The Moon's gravity is about one-sixth of Earth's.
The Moon likely formed from debris after a Mars-sized object smashed into the young Earth.
The Moon has no real atmosphere, so its sky is black even during the day.
The dark patches on the Moon are ancient lava plains called maria, meaning "seas."
Moon dust is sharp and clingy. Apollo astronauts said it smelled like spent gunpowder.
The Moon has water ice in permanently shadowed craters near its poles.
The far side of the Moon isn't dark. It gets just as much sunlight as the near side.
China's Chang'e 4 made the first soft landing on the far side of the Moon in 2019.
A solar eclipse happens because the Moon is about 400 times smaller than the Sun but also about 400 times closer.
Total solar eclipses won't last forever. As the Moon drifts away, it will one day be too small to cover the Sun completely.
During a total lunar eclipse, the Moon turns reddish. It's sometimes called a blood moon.
Earth's shadow on the Moon during an eclipse is curved, one early clue that Earth is round.
The Moon is the only place beyond Earth where humans have set foot.
The last people to walk on the Moon were the crew of Apollo 17, in December 1972.
Apollo astronauts left mirrors on the Moon. Scientists still bounce lasers off them to measure the distance.
There are about 96 bags of human waste left on the Moon from the Apollo missions.
A golf ball hit on the Moon by Alan Shepard in 1971 is still up there.
Ganymede, Titan, Callisto and Io are all bigger than our Moon. Ganymede and Titan are bigger than Mercury.
Europa's ice shell may be 15 to 25 km thick, with an ocean beneath that could hold more water than all of Earth's oceans.
Enceladus is one of the most reflective objects in the solar system because of its fresh ice.
The planets all orbit the Sun in roughly the same flat plane, a leftover from the disc they formed in.
Venus and Uranus are the only planets that spin in the opposite direction to most.
Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune have no solid surface to stand on.
Uranus and Neptune are called ice giants because they contain lots of water, ammonia and methane ices.
Neptune's blue colour comes partly from methane in its atmosphere.
The Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune is a huge ring of icy objects, including Pluto.
The Oort Cloud, a giant shell of icy bodies, may surround the solar system far beyond Pluto.
Many long-period comets are thought to come from the Oort Cloud.
Astronauts on the ISS see the Sun rise or set roughly every 45 minutes.
The ISS travels at about 28,000 km/h.
The ISS is about the size of a football field, including its solar panels.
The ISS has been continuously occupied by humans since November 2000.
You can sometimes spot the ISS from Earth with your bare eyes. It looks like a bright, fast-moving star.
Astronauts on the ISS drink water recycled from sweat, breath moisture and urine.
In space, tears don't fall. They stick to your eyes in a ball.
Astronauts can't burp properly in space, because gas and liquid don't separate in the stomach.
Without gravity, fluids shift towards the head, making astronauts' faces look puffy.
Astronauts lose bone and muscle mass in space, so they exercise about two hours a day.
Astronauts sleep in sleeping bags attached to the wall so they don't float around.
In space, your sense of taste can dull, so many astronauts love spicy food and hot sauce.
Food crumbs are dangerous in space because they can float into equipment or eyes. That's why tortillas are popular instead of bread.
Astronauts' hair and nails keep growing in space, so they cut them near a vacuum hose.
A spacesuit can take about 45 minutes or more to put on with help.
NASA's spacesuits for spacewalks have cost millions of dollars each.
The first spacewalk was made by Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov in 1965.
Leonov's suit ballooned in the vacuum of space, and he had to let air out to squeeze back inside.
Apollo 13's oxygen tank exploded in 1970, but the crew made it home safely.
"Houston, we've had a problem" is what the Apollo 13 crew actually said.
The Apollo 11 computer was far less powerful than a modern calculator.
The Saturn V rocket that took astronauts to the Moon is still one of the most powerful rockets ever launched.
Michael Collins orbited the Moon alone while Armstrong and Aldrin walked on it.
Buzz Aldrin used a felt-tip pen to fix a broken switch so Apollo 11 could take off from the Moon.
The US flags planted on the Moon have probably been bleached white by sunlight.
Sputnik 1, launched in 1957, was the first artificial satellite. It was about the size of a beach ball.
There are thousands of active satellites orbiting Earth today.
Space junk, from old satellites and rocket parts, is a growing problem in Earth's orbit.
Even a tiny paint fleck in orbit can hit hard enough to chip a spacecraft window.
India's ISRO launched 104 satellites on a single rocket in 2017, a record at the time.
Mangalyaan, India's Mars mission, cost less than many Hollywood space movies.
ISRO's first rocket parts were famously carried by bicycle in the 1960s.
Kalpana Chawla was the first woman of Indian origin to go to space, in 1997.
Sunita Williams, an astronaut of Indian descent, has spent hundreds of days in space.
Aditya-L1 is India's first mission to study the Sun.
Shubhanshu Shukla became the first Indian astronaut to visit the ISS, in 2025.
India's Gaganyaan programme aims to launch Indian astronauts on an Indian rocket.
Chandrayaan-1 helped confirm water molecules on the Moon in 2009.
Chandrayaan-3's landing site is named Shiv Shakti Point.
NASA's Parker Solar Probe is the fastest human-made object ever, flying close to the Sun.
The Parker Solar Probe has flown through the Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona.
The Voyager probes were launched in 1977 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment.
Voyager 1 took the "Pale Blue Dot" photo in 1990, showing Earth as a tiny speck.
The New Horizons probe carries some of the ashes of Clyde Tombaugh, who discovered Pluto.
The Rosetta mission landed a probe, Philae, on a comet in 2014.
Japan's Hayabusa2 brought back samples from the asteroid Ryugu.
NASA's OSIRIS-REx collected samples from the asteroid Bennu and returned them to Earth in 2023.
NASA's DART mission crashed into an asteroid in 2022 and changed its orbit, testing planetary defence.
The Hubble telescope was launched with a flawed mirror. Astronauts fixed it in space in 1993.
The James Webb Space Telescope's mirror is made of 18 gold-coated hexagonal segments.
Webb's sunshield is about the size of a tennis court.
Webb sees in infrared, letting it peer through dust and look back to the early universe.
The Spitzer and Kepler telescopes helped discover thousands of planets around other stars.
Kepler found that small planets around other stars are common.
SpaceX became the first private company to send astronauts to the ISS, in 2020.
Reusable rockets that land themselves upright are now routine.
The first tourist to visit space paid for a trip to the ISS in 2001.
A Tesla car and a mannequin called "Starman" were launched into orbit around the Sun in 2018.
Astronauts brought back about 382 kg of Moon rock and soil during the Apollo missions.
Some Moon rocks are older than almost any rocks found on Earth.
Astronauts in orbit aren't weightless because there's no gravity. They're constantly falling around Earth.
At the ISS's height, gravity is still about 90% as strong as on the ground.
Astronauts use special toilets with suction instead of gravity.
The first meal eaten on the Moon was by Apollo 11's crew, and it included bacon squares.
Laika's flight helped prove that living things could survive launch and orbit.
Ham the chimpanzee flew into space in 1961, before the first American astronaut.
Fruit flies were the first animals launched to space, in 1947.
Tardigrades have survived exposure to the vacuum of space in experiments.
Plants have been grown on the ISS, including lettuce that astronauts ate.
Valentina Tereshkova orbited Earth 48 times on her solo mission in 1963.
Mae Jemison became the first African American woman in space in 1992.
The longest single spaceflight by a human lasted about 437 days, by cosmonaut Valeri Polyakov.
More than 600 people have travelled to space.
Some astronauts report a "space smell" after spacewalks, often described as like burnt steak or metal.
Many astronauts describe the "overview effect": a deep sense of awe seeing Earth from space.
From space, astronauts can see city lights, lightning storms and auroras at night.
The Moon landings left behind seismometers, reflectors and lots of equipment that's still there.
Some astronauts have had their wedding rings, family photos and personal items flown to space.
Space agencies are planning to send humans back to the Moon in the coming years through NASA's Artemis programme.
Stars twinkle because their light is bent by moving layers of Earth's atmosphere.
Planets usually don't twinkle as much as stars, because they appear as tiny discs rather than points.
Polaris, the North Star, isn't the brightest star in the sky. It's just almost directly above Earth's North Pole.
Polaris won't always be the North Star. Earth's wobble slowly shifts which star sits above the pole.
In about 12,000 years, the bright star Vega will be close to the North Star position.
Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky.
Sirius is actually two stars: a bright one and a small white dwarf companion.
Many stars in the sky are part of systems with two or more stars.
The Sun is a yellow dwarf star, technically classified as a G-type star.
The Sun isn't really yellow. From space, its light looks white.
Red giants are old stars that have swelled up as they run low on fuel.
The Orion Nebula is a star nursery where new stars are being born. You can see it with binoculars.
Nebulae are giant clouds of gas and dust in space.
The Pillars of Creation are towering columns of gas and dust in the Eagle Nebula, photographed by Hubble and Webb.
The Pleiades, also called the Seven Sisters, is a cluster of young stars visible to the naked eye.
In India, the Pleiades are known as Krittika.
The Big Dipper, called Saptarishi in India, is part of the constellation Ursa Major.
Constellations are patterns we see from Earth. The stars in them are often vastly different distances away.
The zodiac constellations are the ones the Sun appears to pass through during the year.
The Milky Way looks like a band across the sky because we're inside a flat, disc-shaped galaxy.
From a truly dark place, you can see a few thousand stars with your eyes.
Light pollution hides the Milky Way from most of the world's city dwellers.
The Milky Way has spiral arms, and our Sun sits in a smaller arm called the Orion Arm.
Our solar system is about 26,000 light-years from the centre of the galaxy.
The Andromeda Galaxy is the most distant thing most people can see with their bare eyes, about 2.5 million light-years away.
The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are small galaxies that orbit the Milky Way, visible from the Southern Hemisphere.
Galaxies come in different shapes: spiral, elliptical and irregular.
Some galaxies have a bar of stars across their centre. The Milky Way is one of them.
The biggest galaxies can contain trillions of stars.
Galaxy clusters can hold thousands of galaxies bound together by gravity.
Most galaxies have a supermassive black hole at their centre.
Black holes aren't cosmic vacuum cleaners. If the Sun became a black hole of the same mass, Earth would keep orbiting normally.
The first black hole ever confirmed was Cygnus X-1, studied in the 1970s.
Sagittarius A*, the black hole at our galaxy's centre, was photographed for the first time in 2022.
Pulsars are spinning neutron stars that sweep beams of radio waves across space like lighthouses.
The first pulsar signal was so regular that scientists jokingly labelled it "LGM-1," for "little green men."
Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovered the first pulsar in 1967 as a graduate student.
Magnetars are neutron stars with the strongest magnetic fields known in the universe.
A supernova happens roughly once or twice a century in a galaxy like ours.
The last supernova clearly seen in our own galaxy was in 1604, observed by Johannes Kepler.
Supernova 1987A, in a nearby galaxy, was visible to the naked eye from the Southern Hemisphere.
White dwarfs are the leftover cores of stars like the Sun.
When neutron stars collide, they can create gold, platinum and other heavy elements.
In 2017, astronomers saw a neutron star collision with both gravitational waves and light for the first time.
Gamma-ray bursts are the most energetic explosions known in the universe.
Brown dwarfs are "failed stars," too small to sustain fusion like the Sun.
Some stars move so fast they're being flung out of the galaxy. They're called hypervelocity stars.
Variable stars change brightness over time. Some pulse like a heartbeat.
Astronomers use certain pulsing stars, called Cepheids, to measure distances to galaxies.
Edwin Hubble used Cepheid stars to prove that other galaxies exist beyond the Milky Way.
Before the 1920s, many astronomers thought the Milky Way was the entire universe.
The first known exoplanet orbiting a Sun-like star was found in 1995.
Some exoplanets are "hot Jupiters," giant planets orbiting very close to their stars.
Kepler-452b was nicknamed "Earth's cousin" because it orbits a Sun-like star in its habitable zone.
The habitable zone is the region around a star where liquid water could exist on a planet's surface.
A meteor shower happens when Earth passes through debris left by a comet.
The Perseids peak every August. The Geminids peak every December.
The Geminid meteor shower comes from an asteroid, 3200 Phaethon, not a comet.
Meteorites that reach the ground are often older than any rock on Earth.
Some meteorites found on Earth came from Mars, blasted off by ancient impacts.
The Hoba meteorite in Namibia is the largest known single meteorite, about 60 tonnes.
A meteor that exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia, in 2013 shattered windows across the city.
An asteroid impact about 66 million years ago is widely linked to the extinction of the dinosaurs.
The crater from that impact, Chicxulub, lies partly under Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula.
NASA tracks thousands of near-Earth asteroids to check for any danger.
Comets are often called "dirty snowballs" made of ice, dust and rock.
A comet's tail can stretch for millions of kilometres.
Comet Hale-Bopp was visible to the naked eye for a record 18 months in 1996–97.
Astronomers can tell what stars are made of by splitting their light into colours, a method called spectroscopy.
Helium was discovered in the Sun's light before it was found on Earth. Its name comes from Helios, the Greek Sun god.
The Sun has an 11-year cycle of activity, with more sunspots and solar flares at its peak.
Sunspots look dark only because they're cooler than the surrounding surface.
Huge solar storms can disrupt satellites, GPS and power grids on Earth.
The Carrington Event of 1859 was a solar storm so strong that telegraph wires sparked.
The Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona, is millions of degrees, far hotter than its surface. Scientists are still working out why.
A total solar eclipse is the only time most people can see the Sun's corona with their eyes.
Never look at the Sun directly, even during most of an eclipse. Use proper eclipse glasses.
Venus and Jupiter are often the brightest "stars" you'll see in the evening sky. They're planets.
You can see Saturn's rings with a small backyard telescope.
You can see Jupiter's four biggest moons with ordinary binoculars.
Galileo discovered those four moons in 1610. They're called the Galilean moons.
There's a giant cloud of alcohol near the centre of the Milky Way, in a region called Sagittarius B2.
Some molecules in Sagittarius B2 give it a raspberry-like flavour compound, ethyl formate.
Scientists have found water vapour around a quasar billions of light-years away, holding far more water than all of Earth's oceans.
There's a planet, TrES-2b, that reflects less than 1% of the light that hits it, making it darker than coal.
On the exoplanet HD 189733b, scientists think it may rain glass sideways in howling winds.
Some exoplanets may have oceans of lava.
On Neptune and Uranus, extreme pressure may squeeze carbon into diamonds that "rain" down.
Mars has auroras too. In 2024, a rover captured one that would be visible to human eyes.
Jupiter has the brightest auroras in the solar system.
Jupiter gives off more heat than it receives from the Sun.
Saturn's rings are relatively young, perhaps only a few hundred million years old, according to some studies.
Saturn's rings are slowly disappearing, raining down onto the planet.
One of Saturn's moons, Pan, is shaped like a ravioli or a walnut.
Saturn's moon Hyperion looks like a giant sponge.
Saturn's moon Phoebe orbits backwards and may be a captured object from the outer solar system.
Uranus smells like rotten eggs, scientists think, because of hydrogen sulfide in its clouds.
Mercury is shrinking slowly as its core cools.
Mercury has a tail, like a comet, made of sodium.
Earth has had "mini-moons": small asteroids temporarily captured in orbit.
Earth isn't round in a perfect way. It's slightly pear-shaped.
The Moon's surface temperature swings from about 120 °C in sunlight to about −130 °C in darkness.
There's no "dark side of the Moon," just a far side that we never see from Earth.
A day on the Moon, from sunrise to sunrise, lasts about 29.5 Earth days.
The Moon is shrinking a little too, wrinkling its surface as it cools.
Scientists found that some lunar soil can grow plants in lab experiments.
Moon rocks brought back by Apollo are still studied today.
China's Chang'e 5 brought back Moon samples in 2020.
Chang'e 6 brought back the first samples from the far side of the Moon in 2024.
There's a mountain on the asteroid Vesta, Rheasilvia's central peak, about 20 km tall.
The asteroid Psyche may be the exposed metal core of an ancient planet-like body. NASA launched a mission there in 2023.
The asteroid belt's total mass is only about 3% of the Moon's mass.
Some asteroids have their own moons.
The asteroid Dinkinesh has a tiny moon that turned out to be two rocks stuck together.
Comet 67P, studied by Rosetta, smelled like rotten eggs, horse stables and bitter almonds, based on its chemistry.
Interstellar objects, like 'Oumuamua in 2017, have passed through our solar system from other star systems.
'Oumuamua was shaped like a long cigar or a pancake. Scientists still debate its nature.
A second interstellar visitor, comet 2I/Borisov, was found in 2019.
Some stars are so cool you could touch them without being burned, in theory. Some brown dwarfs are about room temperature.
WISE 0855 is a brown dwarf with a temperature below freezing, the coldest known object of its kind.
A star called Methuselah, HD 140283, seems almost as old as the universe itself.
The fastest-spinning known star rotates hundreds of times per second.
The largest known structure in the universe may be a vast wall of galaxies billions of light-years across.
The Boötes Void is an enormous region of space with very few galaxies.
Some galaxies have no detectable dark matter, which puzzles astronomers.
Some galaxies seem to be almost entirely dark matter.
The Milky Way is slowly eating smaller galaxies, like the Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy.
Our galaxy has a warp, like the brim of a hat.
Scientists have found giant bubbles of gas, called the Fermi bubbles, above and below the Milky Way's centre.
The Sun's magnetic field flips every 11 years or so.
The Sun is losing mass constantly, through light and the solar wind.
The Sun's light takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth, but its gravity's effects also travel at the speed of light.
Earth is passing through debris from comets several times a year, causing meteor showers.
About 100 tonnes of space dust may fall on Earth every day, according to older estimates. Newer estimates suggest less.
Micrometeorites can be found on city rooftops.
Every year, a few small meteorites land in India too, and some are collected for research.
If Jupiter had been about 80 times more massive, it could have become a star.
Neptune radiates more than twice as much energy as it gets from the Sun.
The Great Dark Spot on Neptune, seen by Voyager 2, later vanished.
A huge storm on Saturn in 2010–11 wrapped all the way around the planet.
Dust devils on Mars have helped clean rover solar panels, extending missions.
The Opportunity rover was planned for 90 days but lasted almost 15 years.
Opportunity's last message was interpreted as "My battery is low and it's getting dark."
NASA's Spirit rover got stuck in sand in 2009 and was declared lost in 2011.
The Curiosity rover played "Happy Birthday" to itself on Mars in 2013, its first anniversary there.
The Perseverance rover carries a plaque honouring healthcare workers from the COVID-19 pandemic.
Perseverance has collected rock samples that future missions may bring back to Earth.
Some Martian meteorites contain tiny structures once claimed to be fossils of microbes. Most scientists doubt it.
Venus may once have had oceans before a runaway greenhouse effect boiled them away.
Titan's lakes are so still that their surfaces act like mirrors.
Ganymede may have an underground ocean too.
Enceladus's plumes contain salts, organic molecules and phosphorus, some of the ingredients for life.
Pluto may have a hidden ocean beneath its icy shell.
The dwarf planet Haumea is shaped like an egg and spins every four hours.
Sedna, a distant dwarf planet candidate, takes over 10,000 years to orbit the Sun.
Some astronomers think a hidden "Planet Nine" may lurk beyond Neptune, but it hasn't been found.
The Sun is a nearly perfect sphere.
The Sun is made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
The Sun spins faster at its equator than at its poles, because it's not solid.
The Sun takes about 25 days to spin once at its equator.
The Sun's surface temperature is about 5,500 °C.
The Sun produces energy by fusing hydrogen into helium.
The Sun is so massive that it holds the whole solar system together with its gravity.
The Sun's gravity reaches far beyond Pluto, holding the Oort Cloud in orbit.
Without the Sun, Earth's surface would freeze within weeks to months.
Solar eclipses can only happen at new moon. Lunar eclipses can only happen at full moon.
We don't get an eclipse every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted.
A total solar eclipse is visible from any given place only once every few hundred years, on average.
During a total solar eclipse, the temperature can drop noticeably and birds may go quiet.
An annular eclipse happens when the Moon is too far away to cover the Sun completely, leaving a "ring of fire."
The Moon's phases happen because we see different amounts of its sunlit side.
A "supermoon" is a full moon that happens near the Moon's closest approach to Earth.
A supermoon can look about 14% bigger and 30% brighter than a full moon at its farthest point.
The Moon looks bigger near the horizon, but that's an illusion. Its size doesn't change.
The Moon's craters are mostly from ancient impacts, preserved because there's no weather.
The Moon has no global magnetic field today.
The Moon causes most of Earth's ocean tides.
The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day, on average.
A "waxing" moon is growing; a "waning" moon is shrinking.
Earth's shadow is visible at sunset as a dark blue band on the opposite horizon, called the Earth's shadow, topped by a pink "Belt of Venus."
Earthshine is when sunlight reflects off Earth and faintly lights up the dark part of the Moon.
You can see the ISS, satellites and even Starlink trains with your naked eye on clear nights.
Satellites are visible because they reflect sunlight, usually just after sunset or before sunrise.
A "planet parade" is when several planets appear lined up across the sky.
Mercury is hard to see because it's always close to the Sun in our sky.
Mars appears reddish to the naked eye, even from Earth.
Saturn looks like a steady golden star to the naked eye.
Uranus can be just barely seen with the naked eye in very dark skies, if you know exactly where to look.
Neptune can't be seen without a telescope.
The zodiacal light is a faint glow of sunlight scattered by dust in the solar system, seen after dusk or before dawn.
Light pollution makes it hard to see the Milky Way from most cities.
Ladakh's Hanle has India's first Dark Sky Reserve.
The Indian Astronomical Observatory at Hanle is one of the highest observatories in the world.
Your eyes take about 20 to 30 minutes to fully adjust to the dark.
Using red light helps you keep your night vision while stargazing.
Binoculars can show you craters on the Moon and Jupiter's moons.
The best meteor showers can produce dozens of meteors an hour in dark skies.
Meteors usually burn up about 80 to 120 km above the ground.
Fireballs are especially bright meteors, sometimes brighter than Venus.
Sky-watchers in ancient India named the 27 nakshatras, or lunar mansions.
Jantar Mantar in Jaipur has the world's largest stone sundial, accurate to about 2 seconds.
Jantar Mantar observatories were built by Maharaja Jai Singh II in the 1700s.
Aryabhata proposed that Earth rotates on its axis, around 499 CE.
India's first satellite, Aryabhata, was launched in 1975.
ISRO stands for the Indian Space Research Organisation, founded in 1969.
Vikram Sarabhai is considered the father of the Indian space programme.
India's first rocket launch, in 1963, was from Thumba, near Thiruvananthapuram.
Sriharikota in Andhra Pradesh is home to ISRO's main launch centre.
The European Space Agency was founded in 1975.
The first image of Earth from space was taken in 1946 from a rocket.
"Earthrise," taken by Apollo 8 in 1968, is one of the most famous photos ever taken.
"The Blue Marble" photo was taken by the Apollo 17 crew in 1972.
From the Moon, Earth looks about four times wider than the Moon looks from Earth.
Earth doesn't rise and set in the sky as seen from the Moon's near side. It stays in roughly the same spot.
A year on Earth is about 365.25 days, which is why we have leap years.
Earth isn't the same distance from the Sun all year. Its orbit is slightly oval.
Earth moves fastest in its orbit in early January, when it's closest to the Sun.
The seasons are opposite in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
On the equinoxes, day and night are nearly equal everywhere.
The summer solstice in the Northern Hemisphere is the longest day of the year, around 21 June.
At the North Pole, there's one long day and one long night each year.
Earth's atmosphere protects us from most meteors and harmful radiation.
Earth's magnetic field creates the aurora by guiding solar particles towards the poles.
Strong solar storms can push auroras far from the poles. In 2024, auroras were seen as far south as Ladakh.
Earth spins at about 1,670 km/h at the equator, but you don't feel it because everything moves with you.
If Earth stopped spinning suddenly, everything not attached to bedrock would be flung eastward. Luckily, that can't happen.
Earth is the only planet in the solar system with liquid water on its surface.
Earth is the only planet known to have life.
Earth is the fifth-largest planet in the solar system.
Earth's orbit around the Sun is about 940 million km long.
There are thousands of pieces of tracked space debris larger than a softball orbiting Earth.
The Kessler syndrome is a scenario where space debris collisions cause a chain reaction.
The first piece of space debris was Sputnik's rocket body, in 1957.
Some satellites are placed in geostationary orbit, about 36,000 km up, where they stay over the same spot.
GPS uses about 30 satellites orbiting about 20,000 km above Earth.
India's NavIC is its own regional satellite navigation system.
India's INSAT satellites help with weather forecasting and TV broadcasting.
Weather satellites let forecasters track cyclones days before landfall.
Satellites can measure sea level, forest cover and even crop health from space.
Some satellites can see objects smaller than a metre from orbit.
A spoonful of the Sun's core would weigh far more than the same spoonful of water, because the core is extremely dense.
It takes light about 5.5 hours to reach Pluto from the Sun.
Mercury has the most eccentric orbit of the eight planets.
Venus has a thick atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide.
Mars has the largest known volcano and the deepest known canyon in the solar system.
Jupiter's moon Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system.
Saturn's rings are named in order of discovery, using letters.
Neptune's moon Triton is one of the coldest known objects in the solar system, at about −235 °C.
Comets lose material every time they pass near the Sun.
Halley's Comet was last seen in 1986.
There are hundreds of thousands of known asteroids.
The first asteroid ever discovered, Ceres, was found in 1801.
Meteorites are often named after the place where they fall.
The Moon's highest mountains are around 5 km tall, measured from their base.
The James Webb Space Telescope launched on Christmas Day 2021.
The Hubble Space Telescope is named after astronomer Edwin Hubble.
